editorial.headline: A Clear National Opening, a Closed Bali Door for Souvenir Retail
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity welcomes PMA nationally at full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent moratorium closes the registration route for foreign investors.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the retail sale of souvenirs, handicrafts and religious goods made from a wide range of materials. Its territory is deliberately practical rather than narrowly decorative: statues, masks, reliefs, carved names, puppets, frames, lamp shades, trays, bags, baskets, mats, hats, blinds, wall decorations, doormats and fans all sit within its commercial frame. So do smaller keepsake and display articles, from key rings and ashtrays to flower vases, candleholders, medals, trophies, plant pots and ornamental objects made from shells, bone, horn or other materials.

The point is retailing these goods, including an art gallery where the gallery sells the handicraft items concerned. That distinction gives the activity a recognisable commercial centre of gravity: it is for the sale of objects intended as mementos, crafted pieces, decorative articles and religious merchandise, rather than a general description of culture or artistic production. The scope is broad enough to accommodate both everyday souvenir retail and a more curated presentation of craft goods, provided the gallery is selling those goods.

Registration is open across the stated business scales: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. Nationally, the activity is classified as open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a full national opening for PMA participation, supported by the cited Presidential Regulations. It is an important starting point, but it is not the whole operating picture for a founder considering Bali.

In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity through PMA today. At the Large scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for those risk classifications. The moratorium took effect in May 2026. The result is stark but clear: national openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling do not create a PMA registration path for this activity in Bali under the stated provincial rule.
